description: Concrete, author-written lesson narratives with worked illustrative examples; not simulation outputs or a claim of complete coverage.

units.opening: Imagine two small spacecraft freely falling a long way from a black-hole merger. Light exchanged between them records a tiny, changing relative separation. You want to calculate that weak disturbance without solving the complete nonlinear Einstein equations for the entire merging system.

steps.heading: Start with the measurement, not the symbol
steps.text: A metric tells us how spacetime intervals are computed from coordinate differences. In an almost flat region, begin with the flat-spacetime metric ημν. The actual metric is close to that baseline, so write it as gμν = ημν + hμν. The new quantity hμν represents the small difference between the two metric descriptions in the chosen coordinates.

steps.heading: Why keeping only small terms helps
steps.text: The full Einstein equations contain derivatives of the metric multiplied by other metric-dependent quantities. Substituting η + h produces contributions linear in h and higher-order products. If |h| is small in a suitable gauge and region, the linear terms give the leading approximation. This is the same mathematical logic as approximating a complicated function by its first-order Taylor expansion around a known reference state.

steps.heading: What actually travels
steps.text: In a suitable gauge, the linearized vacuum field equations reduce to a wave equation for the trace-reversed perturbation. Wave solutions represent changes propagating at light speed in this approximation. A changing metric component by itself is not always a physical wave: an alternative coordinate choice can change h while describing the same spacetime. Physical tidal effects between nearby freely falling bodies are the crucial observable.

steps.heading: How it connects to a detector
steps.text: A weak passing wave changes the light-travel-time relationship between separated free-falling test masses. Interferometers compare light returning from different arms; their response depends on wave polarization, orientation and the instrument. The theory links a weak spacetime perturbation to a predicted differential strain signal.

example.title: A first-order expansion you can follow
example.text: Suppose one metric component is gxx = 1 + εf(t−z/c), where ε is dimensionless and |εf| ≪ 1. Along a small spatial interval dx with other coordinate differences held fixed, ds² = gxx dx² = [1 + εf]dx². For a positive spatial factor, the corresponding proper-length element is approximately [1 + (ε/2)f] dx, because √(1+u) ≈ 1+u/2 for small u. This is a schematic gauge-dependent illustration of first-order metric perturbation, not a complete detector-response or gauge-invariant distance calculation.

units.boundary: The metric split and simple wave equation assume a weak perturbation about an appropriate background and a particular gauge choice. They cannot by themselves model the strong-field dynamics at merger or justify treating coordinate displacements as observables.

units.opening: Picture a circular binary just before one star collapses. At that instant the companion is at a definite location and both stars have definite velocities. The collapse can change the remnant's mass and impart a directional kick before the companion has time to travel very far.

steps.heading: Take a snapshot of the original orbit
steps.text: Record the relative separation vector r = r_remnant − r_companion and the relative velocity v = v_remnant − v_companion just before the event. Do not replace this by the remnant's speed measured relative to an arbitrary observer: whether the pair stays bound depends on the motion of one body relative to the other.

steps.heading: Apply the event to the relevant quantities
steps.text: Suppose the collapsing star loses some gravitational mass and receives a natal-kick velocity vector w. In the instantaneous impulse approximation, the separation is unchanged during the event. The new relative velocity becomes v′ = v + w if the companion receives no instantaneous kick in the chosen inertial frame. The final gravitational mass is M′ = m_remnant + m_companion.

steps.heading: Check survival, then orbital shape
steps.text: For an isolated Newtonian point-mass pair, compute the specific relative orbital energy ε′ = |v′|²/2 − GM′/r. Negative energy corresponds to a bound orbit, zero to the parabolic boundary, positive to an unbound orbit. For a surviving orbit, use the specific angular momentum vector h′ = r × v′ together with ε′ to obtain the new semi-major axis and eccentricity.

steps.heading: Understand why direction matters
steps.text: A kick in the direction of orbital motion usually raises relative speed; an opposite kick can lower it. A perpendicular kick changes the velocity vector and angular momentum differently. The same kick magnitude can therefore produce different post-collapse eccentricities and survival outcomes depending on phase and orientation.

example.title: Two identical kick magnitudes, two different outcomes
example.text: Use toy units r = 1, GM′ = 1 and a pre-event tangential relative speed v = 1. A tangential kick w = +0.5 gives v′ = 1.5, so ε′ = 1.5²/2 − 1 = +0.125: unbound. The same-magnitude kick w = −0.5 gives v′ = 0.5, so ε′ = 0.5²/2 − 1 = −0.875: bound. Here the direction, not just the kick magnitude, flips the conclusion. These are illustrative post-event units, not a prediction for any observed binary.

units.boundary: The impulse and point-mass model neglects finite-duration mass ejection, interaction with ejecta, tides and detailed collapse physics. In real population synthesis, kick magnitudes and directions are sampled from explicitly stated uncertain prescriptions.

units.opening: Listen to a binary's predicted gravitational-wave signal as it approaches merger. Its cycles become closer together. The change in cycle spacing contains information about how quickly the orbit loses energy compared with how much energy the orbit stores.

steps.heading: Start with two masses on a shrinking orbit
steps.text: For a quasi-circular binary with component masses m₁ and m₂, gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration. To leading Newtonian order, orbital frequency and separation satisfy Ω² = G(m₁+m₂)/r³. As the separation shrinks, the orbital frequency rises. The dominant quadrupolar gravitational-wave frequency is about twice the orbital frequency.

steps.heading: Connect orbital energy to radiated energy
steps.text: The binary's orbital energy becomes more negative as the orbit tightens. Gravitational radiation carries positive energy away. Setting the rate of orbital-energy loss equal to the emitted gravitational-wave power yields an equation for the frequency increase, df/dt. This is why the phase pattern, not merely the signal's loudness, carries mass information.

steps.heading: Why this particular mass combination appears
steps.text: When the leading circular-orbit energy and radiated power are combined, the masses appear as M_c = (m₁m₂)^(3/5)/(m₁+m₂)^(1/5), called the chirp mass. At leading order df/dt is proportional to M_c^(5/3) f^(11/3) in a fixed frame. Larger chirp mass means a faster chirp at the same gravitational-wave frequency, within that approximation.

steps.heading: Read the inference carefully
steps.text: The waveform's phase evolution can constrain chirp mass particularly well. It does not uniquely determine both component masses from that one scalar alone, and observed wave periods are cosmologically redshifted. A claim about the original stars requires additional population and stellar-evolution modeling.

example.title: Compute the chirp mass of an equal-mass binary
example.text: Set m₁ = m₂ = 10 solar masses. Substitution gives M_c = (100)^(3/5)/(20)^(1/5) solar masses = 10/2^(1/5) solar masses ≈ 8.71 solar masses. The chirp mass is neither the total mass (20) nor the mass of either component (10).

units.boundary: The leading formula assumes an isolated, quasi-circular, weak-field inspiral; spin, eccentricity and merger require more complete waveform models. Distinguish source-frame from detector-frame mass.

units.opening: Imagine a giant star expanding around its much smaller companion. In a possible unstable interaction, the companion travels inside the giant's gaseous envelope. Friction-like gravitational interaction with that gas removes orbital energy from the cores' relative orbit.

steps.heading: What has entered what?
steps.text: The expanded donor is not a solid sphere. Its outer layers are gas surrounding a dense core. During common-envelope evolution, the companion and the donor's core move inside gas that can exert gravitational drag and exchange energy and angular momentum with the orbit.

steps.heading: Where does the energy go?
steps.text: As the orbit tightens, its gravitational orbital energy becomes more negative; the released difference can heat, accelerate and help unbind envelope gas. This produces the idea behind simplified envelope-energy prescriptions: compare the energy required to eject the gas with some usable fraction of the orbital energy released.

steps.heading: Why an apparently successful spiral-in can still fail
steps.text: If insufficient energy reaches the gas before the cores collide, the system may merge inside the envelope. If the envelope is ejected in time, the survivors can emerge in a much closer orbit. That closer orbit may later become a compact binary capable of merging under gravitational-wave emission, provided subsequent evolution permits it.

steps.heading: What a population model actually assumes
steps.text: A rapid synthesis code cannot resolve the entire three-dimensional gas flow for every simulated binary. It often uses an efficiency parameter and a binding-energy prescription to approximate the outcome. Varying these assumptions can substantially change predicted post-envelope separations and compact-binary yields.

example.title: An energy ledger, not an automatic survival proof
example.text: Suppose an envelope needs 10 toy energy units to unbind. If the shrinking orbit releases 15 and an assumed efficiency α = 0.6 makes only 9 units usable, the simplified energy budget does not reach the 10-unit requirement. Even if 10 units were available, the calculation alone would not tell you whether the cores fit safely inside the final orbit.

units.boundary: A one-parameter energy budget neglects multidimensional hydrodynamics and possible other energy sources. Its efficiency is a model prescription, not a universally measured constant.

units.opening: Picture one star in a close binary expanding until gas at its surface can flow toward its companion. Rather than thinking of two isolated stars that occasionally trade material, you now need to think about the geometry of their shared gravitational and rotating environment.

steps.heading: Find the geometric boundary
steps.text: In a co-rotating description, each star has a Roche lobe: a region bounded by an effective gravitational equipotential. When the donor's photosphere reaches that boundary, gas can flow through the inner Lagrange region. Roche-lobe overflow is the onset of a transfer pathway; it does not by itself determine whether the exchange stays stable.

steps.heading: Track how the star and boundary change
steps.text: As the donor loses mass, its radius can expand or shrink depending on stellar structure and timescale. The Roche-lobe radius changes too, because mass ratio, orbit and angular momentum evolve. If the donor expands relative to the boundary, overfilling may deepen and transfer can accelerate.

steps.heading: Separate the mass ledger from the orbital ledger
steps.text: In an ideal conservative episode, the donor loses exactly what the accretor gains, so total binary mass is unchanged. In a non-conservative episode, some gas leaves the system and carries angular momentum. Even perfectly conservative exchange can change the separation because the mass ratio and orbital angular-momentum distribution evolve.

steps.heading: Follow the possible later histories
steps.text: Some systems undergo stable transfer, strip an envelope and survive. Other configurations encounter unstable transfer and may enter common-envelope evolution or merge. The outcome depends on the evolutionary state, mass ratio, the star's structural response and the adopted physical prescription.

example.title: One transfer event, two separate accounting questions
example.text: A 12-solar-mass donor loses 4 solar masses and its 6-solar-mass companion accretes 3. Final masses are 8 and 9 solar masses; 1 solar mass left the binary. The new mass ratio is 8/9, but these numbers do not determine the orbital separation until you also specify how much angular momentum the escaping material removed.

units.boundary: Roche geometry is a simplified binary model, and stability cannot be inferred from an instantaneous radius or mass ratio alone. Detailed mass-loss, accretion and angular-momentum prescriptions are required.

units.opening: Imagine wanting to know how many of a million hypothetical newborn binary stars would eventually produce a pair of merging black holes. You cannot observe the entire lifetime of each real system, so you generate many initial binaries and follow model rules through their possible evolutionary histories.

steps.heading: Specify what gets born
steps.text: Draw initial masses, mass ratios, orbital periods, eccentricities and metallicities from documented distributions. If you deliberately oversample rare systems, record appropriate sampling weights so that raw simulated counts are not mistaken for the underlying birth population.

steps.heading: Evolve each system through a sequence of events
steps.text: Apply prescriptions for stellar winds, expansion, Roche-lobe overflow, transfer stability, possible common-envelope phases, collapse and natal kicks. A system may merge early, disrupt at an explosion, remain wide or produce a double compact remnant. An event log can contain many rows for the same binary.

steps.heading: Define the actual outcome of interest
steps.text: A surviving black-hole pair is not automatically a merging source within the age of the Universe. Apply an explicit inspiral-time condition, then summarize distributions of masses, spins, delay times and formation channels, respecting distinct-system identifiers and sampling weights.

steps.heading: Connect predictions to data without skipping observation
steps.text: To compare predicted intrinsic mergers with detections, account for cosmic star formation, birth metallicity, delays, distance/redshift and detector selection. A difference between model and catalog can arise from stellar physics, population normalization or the observation model; raw detected counts do not isolate which.

example.title: Why counting table rows gives a wrong merger fraction
example.text: A toy event log has eight rows representing three distinct simulated binaries; four of those rows belong to the same binary. Suppose only one of the three distinct systems forms a pair that merges within the chosen horizon. The unweighted successful-system fraction is 1/3, not 1/8 or 4/8. A physical formation efficiency additionally requires the represented formed-stellar-mass normalization and any sampling weights.

units.boundary: Rapid population synthesis uses approximate and uncertain prescriptions, not a direct movie of the Universe. Controlled sensitivity studies and stochastic-convergence checks are needed before interpreting an output trend.

units.opening: Imagine a population containing equal numbers of two kinds of merging binaries. One kind produces stronger signals at the same distance and orientation. Your detector records many more of that kind, even though their true cosmic abundance is equal.

steps.heading: Start with the underlying population
steps.text: The intrinsic merger distribution describes the systems that actually merge, whether or not any detector observes them. A finite observing run does not survey the entire Universe equally: detectable strain depends on source masses, spins, distance, inclination and a time-dependent instrument response.

steps.heading: Model the filter explicitly
steps.text: A detection probability p_det(θ) describes how likely a source with properties θ is to meet a specified detection criterion. It can be estimated with simulated signal injections into real or representative detector noise. It is not an independent probability that the source physically exists.

steps.heading: See how the histogram changes
steps.text: If one class is detected with probability 0.8 and another with probability 0.2, equal intrinsic numbers generate a four-to-one expected ratio in the observed catalog. An inference that mistakes this detected distribution for the intrinsic distribution would incorrectly claim one type forms four times more often.

steps.heading: Undo the filter carefully
steps.text: Population inference compares a forward prediction passed through the detection process with the actual catalog, while also accounting for measurement uncertainties, observing exposure and the fact that the analysis is conditioned on detection. Raw inverse-probability weights can illustrate the idea but are not a substitute for a complete astrophysical rate likelihood.

example.title: An observed ratio is not automatically a formation ratio
example.text: Suppose 100 intrinsic events of class A and 100 of class B occur during a toy observing window. With efficiencies 0.8 and 0.2, expected observed counts are 80 and 20. The catalog ratio 4:1 differs from the intrinsic ratio 1:1 without any change in the Universe's actual population.

units.boundary: The model must specify a detector network, observing run, search method and source distribution. Euclidean volume approximations become inadequate when cosmology, duty cycles and detector antenna patterns matter.

units.opening: Picture receiving a short gravitational-wave signal from two black holes just before merger. You can estimate properties of those compact objects, but there is no recording of their original stars. The research problem is how to infer what happened during the millions or billions of years that preceded the final signal.

steps.heading: Begin at the observed end of the story
steps.text: A waveform constrains merger properties such as redshifted masses and aspects of the spins, distance and orientation with measurement uncertainties. Those are observations of a late evolutionary stage, not direct measurements of stellar birth masses or past mass-transfer events.

steps.heading: Run the physical story forward
steps.text: Model many possible progenitor populations. Evolve massive stars through winds, binary interactions, core collapse and kicks; propagate surviving compact binaries through gravitational-wave inspiral and cosmic delay times. Each set of prescriptions predicts a distribution of merger properties.

steps.heading: Pass the prediction through a detector
steps.text: Account for redshift, orientation, instrument sensitivity and the analysis selection function. Only then compare predicted detections to an observed catalog. A good match to the raw catalog alone may result from detector filtering rather than correct underlying stellar physics.

steps.heading: Work backward statistically, not as a single lookup
steps.text: Compare multiple forward-model predictions with observations. A distribution of detected masses, spins and merger rates may constrain combinations of formation assumptions, but distinct histories can generate overlapping signals. Report which assumptions the data inform and which remain degenerate.

example.title: A simple ambiguity
example.text: Suppose two stellar-evolution prescriptions both predict merging black holes with comparable masses, but via different wind and mass-transfer histories. Measuring one binary's two merger masses will not distinguish these histories uniquely. Their predicted mass distribution, spin distribution, merger-rate evolution and selection effects must be compared over many events.

units.boundary: Conclusions about progenitors are conditional on astrophysical models, cosmic history, detection efficiencies and waveform inference. They should not be presented as direct memories encoded uniquely in a single signal.

units.opening: Suppose a wave reaches Earth from a binary merging today, but its two original stars formed several billion years earlier. Counting only stars born today would miss that event, because formation and merger occur at different times.

steps.heading: Assign two clocks to every binary
steps.text: One clock marks the birth of the progenitor stellar system; another marks the compact-binary merger. Their elapsed difference is a delay time, which may include stellar evolution and later inspiral depending on the model definition.

steps.heading: Build the birth history
steps.text: The cosmic star-formation rate describes how much stellar mass forms at different epochs, while the metallicity distribution describes the range of birth compositions. Binary-formation efficiency and survival depend on those conditions and the assumed stellar-evolution prescriptions.

steps.heading: Shift births forward by their delays
steps.text: For a toy single-delay population, each cohort merges a fixed interval after it forms. Real populations contain a delay-time distribution, so a merger-rate history combines contributions from many earlier formation epochs. This is why the merger-rate peak need not coincide with the star-formation peak.

steps.heading: Convert intrinsic events to predicted detections
steps.text: The physical rate density is commonly expressed per comoving volume per source-frame time. Predicted detector counts also require the cosmological volume element, the factor converting source-frame time to observer-frame time, the observing schedule and the detection efficiency.

example.title: Two cohorts and a fixed delay
example.text: In a toy universe, 10 merger-capable systems form at cosmic time 2 Gyr and 20 at 5 Gyr. If all merge after a 4-Gyr delay, they merge at times 6 and 9 Gyr respectively. The merger history is shifted relative to the birth history even though the underlying birth cohorts are unchanged.

units.boundary: This toy construction ignores distributions in mass, metallicity, star formation, delay and detection. Cosmological comparisons must state which time coordinate and rate normalization they use.

units.opening: Imagine a detector catalog with fifty merger candidates. Each event has uncertain masses and spins; some kinds of mergers are much easier to detect. You want to learn the properties of the underlying population without pretending every candidate gives one exact pair of masses.

steps.heading: Distinguish the three distributions
steps.text: An event-level likelihood describes which source parameters fit the detector data. An analysis prior represents assumptions used in that event's parameter estimation. Combining the two produces the event posterior; a population distribution is yet another model describing how source parameters vary across events.

steps.heading: Write a forward population model
steps.text: Introduce hyperparameters Λ, such as a mass-distribution slope or a formation-channel mixture fraction. This model predicts the relative frequency of different event parameters θ. Predict how those events would be measured, rather than fitting a histogram of posterior medians.

steps.heading: Account for the fact that you saw detected events
steps.text: Detection conditions change the population of events that enters the catalog. The likelihood for an observed sample requires a selection term computed for the population model and observing procedure; otherwise a model might fit the easiest-to-detect sources while misrepresenting the intrinsic distribution.

steps.heading: Interpret the result within its assumptions
steps.text: Combine the information from events, including measurement uncertainties and proper accounting for the event-level priors. The resulting constraints on Λ depend on the chosen model family, priors and selection calculation. Comparing different families and conducting sensitivity checks helps expose degeneracy.

example.title: A misleading detected mixture
example.text: Suppose source classes A and B have intrinsic fractions 0.3 and 0.7 but detection probabilities 0.9 and 0.1. Their expected detected contributions are 0.27 and 0.07. A contributes 0.27/(0.27+0.07) ≈ 79% of detections despite being only 30% of the intrinsic population.

units.boundary: Posterior preference among a chosen set of models is not proof that the inferred progenitor pathway is uniquely true. Selection modeling, event priors and neglected alternatives must be reported.

units.opening: Imagine looking at a detector strain time series: its signal grows and the peaks come closer together. Rather than memorizing labels for waveform phases, ask what motion of the binary would make both of those changes appear.

steps.heading: Relate orbit and periodic strain
steps.text: Two masses orbit a shared center of mass. Their changing mass quadrupole produces gravitational radiation. In the leading quasi-circular approximation, the strongest oscillatory component has a frequency approximately twice the orbital frequency.

steps.heading: Follow the shrinking orbit
steps.text: Radiation removes orbital energy and angular momentum. In the idealized isolated inspiral, separation decreases and orbital frequency rises. The characteristic gravitational-wave frequency rises too; the spacing between successive cycles in a time-domain plot becomes shorter.

steps.heading: Separate inspiral, merger and ringdown
steps.text: The early inspiral is amenable to perturbative approximations when gravity is comparatively weak and motion is not too relativistic. Near merger, strong-field dynamics require more complete models. After two black holes merge, the perturbed remnant settles through damped oscillations called ringdown.

steps.heading: Read what an instrument actually records
steps.text: The detector responds to a projection of the source's wave polarizations, influenced by sky location, inclination, distance and instrumental noise. A strain pattern is therefore not a direct plot of either object's physical trajectory, even though waveform models connect the two.

example.title: Frequency in a circular orbit
example.text: If a quasi-circular compact binary has orbital frequency 35 Hz, its leading quadrupolar gravitational-wave frequency is approximately 70 Hz. As the binary loses energy and inspirals, both frequencies rise. This relation is leading-order; a complete merger waveform includes additional modes and strong-field behavior.

units.boundary: Waveform interpretation depends on approximations, the adopted mass/spin/eccentricity model and detector calibration. Do not interpret all transient detector noise as astrophysical waveforms.

units.opening: Take two stars orbiting each other. One begins losing matter in a wind, and later gas flows toward its companion. The orbit can widen during one stage and shrink during another even though 'mass loss' appears in both descriptions.

steps.heading: Track two objects rather than one scalar mass
steps.text: Record the masses m₁ and m₂, relative separation, eccentricity and orbital angular momentum. In an isolated Newtonian two-body orbit, masses and orbital elements determine energy and angular momentum, but interactive evolution changes the binary's internal energy budget.

steps.heading: Ask what happens to escaping matter
steps.text: Matter leaving a star might be captured by the companion or escape altogether. Escaping gas may remove angular momentum, while tides, winds and drag can exchange energy with the orbit. Merely knowing that one star lost one solar mass does not identify the orbital response.

steps.heading: Separate slow, fast and dissipative events
steps.text: Slow mass changes can allow a different orbital response than an impulsive supernova. During Roche-lobe overflow, the donor's radius and its effective lobe change with mass ratio and angular-momentum transport. A common-envelope spiral-in dissipates orbital energy into gas.

steps.heading: Connect the resulting orbit to a later merger
steps.text: After the compact remnants form, a wide binary may remain bound yet take longer than a cosmic age to merge. A close binary can have a much shorter gravitational-wave inspiral time. Formation survival and merger-within-a-horizon are distinct filters.

example.title: One missing piece in an orbit calculation
example.text: An initial binary has 10 and 8 solar masses. The donor loses 3, the companion accretes 2, and 1 escapes, leaving masses 7 and 10. You can calculate this mass ledger exactly, but the final separation still depends on the angular momentum carried by the escaping mass and the interaction history.

units.boundary: Isolated Keplerian conservation cannot simply be applied to an interacting two-star subsystem without accounting for energy and angular momentum exchanged with gas or other bodies.

units.opening: Picture two stars moving in a wide orbit. You want to know how much energy the binary must lose before its orbit can become tight enough to make a compact merger plausible. Rather than adding two unrelated stellar kinetic energies, describe the motion of one star relative to the other.

steps.heading: Replace two trajectories by their relative motion
steps.text: Let r be the separation and v the relative velocity. For two Newtonian point masses m₁ and m₂, define total mass M=m₁+m₂ and reduced mass μ=m₁m₂/M. The relative kinetic energy is μv²/2, while the interaction potential, with zero chosen at infinite separation, is −Gm₁m₂/r.

steps.heading: Find the circular reference orbit
steps.text: For a circular relative orbit, the gravitational attraction Gm₁m₂/r² provides the reduced-mass centripetal force μv²/r. Cancel μ and rearrange to obtain v²=GM/r. Substituting into K=μv²/2 gives K=Gm₁m₂/(2r), exactly half the magnitude of the interaction potential in this idealized circular case.

steps.heading: Generalize energy to the size of a bound Kepler orbit
steps.text: Adding the circular terms gives E=−Gm₁m₂/(2r). For a bound Keplerian ellipse, the time-independent orbital energy is E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a), where a is the semi-major axis; it does not depend on the eccentricity at fixed component masses and a. More negative E describes a more tightly bound binary under the stated potential convention.

steps.heading: Connect the ledger to binary evolution
steps.text: If the orbit shrinks from aᵢ to a𝒇 at fixed masses, ΔE_orb=−Gm₁m₂(1/a𝒇−1/aᵢ)/2. This is negative, meaning orbital energy decreased; a gas envelope or gravitational radiation may receive the released positive energy. If masses change or gas exerts drag, you must account for their energy and angular-momentum exchange rather than applying isolated-orbit conservation blindly.

example.title: Why halving the orbit releases energy
example.text: In units with Gm₁m₂=1, the energy at aᵢ=4 is −1/8. At a𝒇=2 it is −1/4. The change in orbital energy is −1/8, so 1/8 unit of positive energy was released to another part of the system in an energy-conserving account. The more negative final energy is not a claim that physical energy disappeared; it reflects the chosen zero of gravitational potential.

units.boundary: Newtonian two-point-mass energy assumes the masses are sufficiently compact, the interaction is approximately isolated and gravity is represented by −Gm₁m₂/r. A common envelope, mass ejection and strong-field inspiral require additional physics and do not preserve binary orbital energy separately.

units.opening: Picture a giant donor star in a close binary. As it expands, gas near the point between the stars begins to feel the companion's gravity strongly. To predict when matter can begin streaming toward the companion, you need a boundary defined by the binary's combined gravity and rotation, not merely the donor's isolated surface escape speed.

steps.heading: Adopt the rotating point of view
steps.text: In a frame rotating with a nearly circular binary, the stars are approximately stationary while a test parcel experiences gravitational attraction toward both masses together with a centrifugal contribution. These define an effective Roche potential. Surfaces of equal effective potential can enclose regions around each star.

steps.heading: Locate the critical passage between the stars
steps.text: The inner Lagrange point L₁ lies between the bodies where the effective potential has a saddle. The critical equipotential passing through L₁ defines a lobe around each star. When a donor expands toward that boundary, gas near L₁ can follow a flow toward the companion rather than remain confined around the donor.

steps.heading: Replace the complicated lobe shape by a useful radius
steps.text: For an idealized circular synchronized binary, Eggleton's fitting expression gives the donor's volume-equivalent Roche radius: R_L/a≈0.49q^(2/3)/[0.6q^(2/3)+ln(1+q^(1/3))], where q=M_donor/M_accretor and a is the instantaneous separation. This is a geometric approximation, not a claim that the lobe is literally a sphere.

steps.heading: Separate the onset of overflow from its dynamical fate
steps.text: Compare R_donor and R_L. When R_donor reaches or exceeds the effective boundary, Roche-lobe overflow can begin. To predict whether the exchange stabilizes or accelerates, compare how the donor's structure responds to mass loss with how the lobe radius changes through mass and angular-momentum transfer; the overflow condition alone does not decide stability.

example.title: Equal-mass lobe size
example.text: For q=1, q^(1/3)=q^(2/3)=1, giving R_L/a≈0.49/(0.6+ln2)≈0.379. At separation a=10 solar radii, each volume-equivalent Roche radius is about 3.79 solar radii. A donor radius of 4 solar radii therefore exceeds its approximate lobe radius in this idealized configuration, suggesting overflow may begin; a full interaction calculation is still needed.

units.boundary: The fitting formula assumes an equilibrium Roche geometry for a circular synchronized point-mass binary. Strong eccentricity, rapid non-synchronous rotation, extended atmospheres and dynamical gas flows complicate this picture; lobe contact does not quantify a transfer rate or guarantee a common envelope.

units.opening: Imagine two otherwise similar massive stars born with different abundances of elements heavier than helium. Before either collapses, its radiation can push on ions in the atmosphere and carry material away. Over millions of years, those winds can change the mass that reaches core collapse and therefore the possible compact-remnant population.

steps.heading: Follow the outgoing light rather than naming a wind rate
steps.text: Photons carry momentum. In a hot luminous star, many metal ions absorb and scatter radiation through spectral lines, allowing radiative momentum to accelerate atmospheric material. The collective transfer of momentum can sustain an outflow; metal-line opacity therefore connects chemical composition to a star's ability to drive some types of winds.

steps.heading: Track the evolving stellar mass
steps.text: Define a positive mass-loss rate Ṁ_loss=−dM_star/dt. The stellar mass remaining after an interval is M(t)=M₀−∫Ṁ_loss(t′)dt′. A model may compute Ṁ_loss from luminosity, temperature, composition and other properties; it should not silently hold a time-dependent stellar parameter constant over an entire evolutionary history.

steps.heading: Connect winds to orbit and collapse
steps.text: Matter lost from the star changes its envelope and its pre-collapse mass. If the material escapes the binary it can also carry orbital angular momentum, possibly widening or otherwise changing the orbit depending on the loss geometry and timescale. For a compact-remnant prediction, distinguish material ejected in winds before collapse from mass lost and neutrinos emitted during the collapse event itself.

steps.heading: Treat metallicity dependence as a conditional physical claim
steps.text: Hot-star line-driven wind prescriptions often describe stronger winds at higher metallicity within a specified temperature and evolutionary regime. Different wind mechanisms, ionization states, clumping corrections and evolutionary phases need not obey one universal power law. In population synthesis, vary the adopted prescription before attributing a predicted remnant-mass difference solely to metallicity.

example.title: Integrate a prescribed toy wind
example.text: A toy star begins at 30 solar masses and loses mass at a constant positive rate of 10⁻⁶ solar masses per year for 2×10⁶ years. The prescribed wind removes 2 solar masses, giving 28 solar masses remaining. This calculation does not predict the actual star's luminosity, fuel use, collapse time or remnant mass: its rate and duration were hypothetical fixed inputs.

units.boundary: Do not infer a universal metallicity exponent from this explanation. Line-driven winds are best understood within their stellar-temperature and luminosity regimes, while cool-star and eruptive outflows may depend on different mechanisms. Real stellar tracks solve coupled structure and composition evolution.

units.opening: Imagine a compact binary whose stars have already collapsed into two black holes. Unlike an isolated Kepler orbit, the binary loses energy and angular momentum by producing gravitational waves. The crucial research question is whether the pair spirals together on a time scale comparable to its age or remains too widely separated to merge.

steps.heading: Calculate how orbital energy depends on separation
steps.text: For a Newtonian quasi-circular pair of point masses, E_orb=−Gm₁m₂/(2a). A reduction in a makes E more negative. Gravitational radiation carries positive energy away, so dE_orb/dt is negative; by the chain rule dE/dt=(dE/da)(da/dt), where dE/da=Gm₁m₂/(2a²)>0.

steps.heading: Use the leading quadrupolar energy-loss approximation
steps.text: At lowest order for a circular point-mass binary, the gravitational-wave power is P_GW=(32/5)G⁴ μ²M³/(c⁵a⁵), with M=m₁+m₂ and μ=m₁m₂/M. Equate dE/dt=−P_GW and solve for da/dt=−(64/5)G³m₁m₂M/(c⁵a³). The negative sign shows separation shrinks in this isolated model.

steps.heading: Integrate the remaining time carefully
steps.text: Separate variables: a³ da=−K dt where K=(64/5)G³m₁m₂M/c⁵. Integrating from initial a₀ to the formal a=0 limit gives t_leading=5c⁵a₀⁴/[256G³m₁m₂M]. This quartic dependence means that moderately wider systems can have much longer leading-order inspiral times.

steps.heading: Distinguish a merger candidate from a surviving binary
steps.text: Formation calculations may produce a bound double compact object with a separation too wide for it to merge within a chosen cosmic horizon. Apply an inspiral-time criterion separately from bound survival. For eccentric orbits, radiation losses and the merger time depend on eccentricity as well as the initial semi-major axis; the circular expression is not a general eccentric-binary formula.

example.title: Why modestly changing separation matters
example.text: Hold both compact masses fixed and compare circular pairs at a and 2a. Since the leading time scales as a⁴, the pair at 2a has 2⁴=16 times the inspiral time of the pair at a. If the first toy system has a calculated leading time of 0.5 Gyr, the second has 8 Gyr under the same approximation. This is why the post-common-envelope separation strongly affects merger predictions.

units.boundary: The leading quadrupole and Newtonian orbital-energy treatment breaks down close to merger, and real sources can be eccentric or spinning. The a→0 integral is a convenient leading-order extrapolation, not an exact strong-field plunge or ringdown time. Cosmological age comparisons require formation epoch and redshift.

units.opening: Imagine a passing gravitational wave arriving at a detector with two perpendicular arms. A test mass in each arm is suspended so that, over the measurement band, the interferometer can compare how the passing wave changes the relative light-travel times along the two directions. The recorded signal is not a photograph of a black hole orbit.

steps.heading: Start with the laser phase difference
steps.text: A laser beam is split between two long arms, reflected from test masses and recombined. The returning light waves interfere according to their relative phase. A change in the differential optical path length changes that interference and can be inferred from the measured light signal.

steps.heading: Relate strain to differential arm response
steps.text: For a suitable wave orientation and polarization in a simple long-wavelength picture, a dimensionless strain h corresponds to an order-h fractional differential length change: ΔL/L≈h up to the interferometer response convention. The antenna response depends on source direction, polarization and detector orientation. A single measured differential signal does not separately reveal every source and sky parameter.

steps.heading: Distinguish a signal from detector noise
steps.text: The measured strain channel contains instrument noise as well as any astrophysical signal. Seismic motion, thermal noise and quantum measurement noise dominate different frequency ranges. Searching for a compact-binary waveform therefore requires calibrated instrument response, noise modeling and a detection procedure rather than inspecting one oscillation by eye.

steps.heading: Connect measured strain to astrophysical inference
steps.text: Waveform templates predict the time-dependent strain for source parameters such as masses, spins, distance and orientation. Comparing calibrated data with a waveform model constrains those parameters with uncertainty; a population analysis must also account for sources whose strain patterns would not meet the detection threshold.

example.title: An order-of-magnitude arm displacement
example.text: For an illustrative arm length L=4 km and a strain scale h=10⁻²¹, the product hL is 4×10⁻¹⁸ m. This is only a scale estimate for a favorable response, not the actual optical signal in a LIGO detector: mirror response, light storage, frequency, direction and polarization modify the measurement.

units.boundary: A real detector does not simply read one permanent ruler change; it is a calibrated dynamic optical instrument with frequency-dependent response and noise. The arm-length product is an intuition, not a complete interferometer transfer function or an argument for a detection claim.

units.opening: Imagine you want to estimate what fraction of a large hypothetical binary population survives a supernova. You cannot evolve every conceivable combination of masses and kicks. Instead, you draw a finite collection of initial conditions from specified distributions, run a model on each, and use the outcomes as a sample.

steps.heading: Define the population before drawing numbers
steps.text: A random sample is only meaningful relative to a chosen probability model. Specify distributions for each variable, such as component masses, orbital separation, kick magnitude and kick direction. If you deliberately oversample rare progenitors, record the sampling design and weights rather than treating the raw simulated frequencies as the birth frequencies.

steps.heading: Make the random experiment repeatable
steps.text: Use a documented pseudo-random-number generator and record its seed, software version, input distributions and filtering rules. The same seed reproduces the same toy draws with the same implementation, which is useful for debugging; it does not make the modeled physics correct or establish that one seed represents the full uncertainty.

steps.heading: Estimate a proportion and its sampling variability
steps.text: For N independent Bernoulli outcomes Xᵢ∈{0,1} under simple random sampling, p̂=(∑Xᵢ)/N estimates the underlying model probability. Its estimated standard error is approximately sqrt[p̂(1−p̂)/N]. The formula assumes independent identically distributed indicator draws and ignores additional model, weighting and measurement uncertainty.

steps.heading: Compare model assumptions without confusing noise for physics
steps.text: When testing two kick prescriptions, hold the physical question and relevant inputs constant while varying the prescription. Compare their outcome distributions over enough independent samples; common random numbers may help reduce Monte Carlo variation in paired designs. Report effect sizes and sampling variability before interpreting a small difference as a physical consequence.

example.title: A reproducible toy survival estimate
example.text: Draw N=100 independent toy systems and suppose 36 meet the stipulated survival condition. Then p̂=36/100=0.36 and the plug-in standard error is sqrt(0.36×0.64/100)=0.048. Reporting 36%±4.8 percentage points as an approximate one-standard-error sampling summary does not account for the uncertainty in the selected astrophysical model or any oversampling weights.

units.boundary: The binomial standard-error formula is not generally correct for correlated trajectories, importance sampling, clustered draws or uncertain weights. The sample distribution models only the assumptions entered; increasing N reduces Monte Carlo noise but cannot eliminate systematic model misspecification.

units.opening: Imagine you deliberately simulate many rare massive binaries because those are the systems most likely to produce the mergers you care about. If you simply count simulated rows, the rare systems may look much more common than they are among genuinely forming stars. Sampling weights are the bridge between your simulation design and the target population.

steps.heading: Distinguish sample frequency from population frequency
steps.text: A simulation may draw initial states from a proposal distribution q(x) while the intended birth population follows p(x). If the support is appropriate, a standard importance weight is proportional to p(x)/q(x). The exact normalized weight convention depends on the simulation design and whether the target is an expectation, a rate or a mass-normalized yield.

steps.heading: Keep system identifiers separate from event rows
steps.text: An evolutionary history can contain many rows for one binary, corresponding to wind, transfer, collapse and compact-binary stages. Counting rows as if they were independently sampled systems overweights systems with more recorded events. First identify distinct simulated binaries and define one outcome and one consistent statistical weight per system for the summary of interest.

steps.heading: Compute weighted summaries with an explicit denominator
steps.text: For systems i with outcome indicator Iᵢ and nonnegative population weights wᵢ, a normalized weighted fraction is p̂_w=(∑wᵢIᵢ)/(∑wᵢ). A mass-normalized formation efficiency instead requires a denominator representing formed stellar mass under the target population; ∑wᵢ alone may not have the units or normalization required.

steps.heading: Treat uncertainty and normalization separately
steps.text: A highly uneven weight distribution can make the effective sample size much smaller than the number of simulated systems. One diagnostic is N_eff=(∑wᵢ)²/∑wᵢ². This is an indicator of weight concentration, not a complete uncertainty estimate; astrophysical prescription uncertainty and output-selection effects need separate study.

example.title: Why an unweighted fraction can be misleading
example.text: Two distinct systems have outcomes I₁=1 and I₂=0 and target-population weights w₁=1 and w₂=9. The unweighted success fraction is 1/2=50%, but the normalized weighted fraction is (1×1+9×0)/(1+9)=0.10, or 10%. Neither number alone is a physical merger rate: the target birth normalization and relevant delays and detection selection are still missing.

units.boundary: Never assign weights without defining the sampling and target distributions. The normalized weighted fraction assumes each system’s weight represents its intended share of the target population. A physical rate per formed stellar mass and a detected-event count have different denominators and cannot be substituted for each other.

units.opening: Imagine a star-forming region that produces many binary progenitors in a short burst. Some compact pairs merge relatively quickly; others take billions of years. Even though all progenitors formed together, their mergers are spread across cosmic time because every surviving system has its own evolutionary and inspiral delay.

steps.heading: Put birth and merger on a common time axis
steps.text: Let t_b be a progenitor formation time and t_m its merger time. Define the delay τ=t_m−t_b, with τ≥0 under the model. State whether τ includes both stellar evolution and post-compact-object inspiral; mixing a compact-binary-only delay with a birth-to-merger delay shifts predicted merger epochs.

steps.heading: Turn many delays into a distribution
steps.text: For a population capable of merging, a normalized delay-time density p(τ) specifies how the eventual merger probability is distributed across delays. If some simulated systems never merge within the adopted horizon, either account for them in an overall formation efficiency or work with an explicitly conditional density over the systems that do merge.

steps.heading: Combine one birth cohort with its later outcomes
steps.text: For a single cohort born at t_b, the distribution of its merger times is the same delay distribution shifted by t_b: t_m=t_b+τ. For an extended formation history F(t), a simplified merger-rate expression is R(t)=∫₀ᵗF(t−τ)η(t−τ)p(τ|t−τ)dτ, with η representing formation-to-merger yield under the chosen population convention.

steps.heading: Connect the distribution to observed detections
steps.text: Real predictions may require metallicity dependence, binary formation efficiency, comoving volume, source-to-observer time conversion and detector selection. A late merger does not prove a late progenitor birth; multiple formation histories combined with different delay distributions can lead to similar merger-rate histories.

example.title: Shift a concrete birth cohort
example.text: Suppose 100 merger-capable binaries form at cosmic time t_b=2 Gyr and, under a toy model, exactly 30 have delay τ=1 Gyr while 70 have delay τ=4 Gyr. Their merger times are t_m=3 Gyr and t_m=6 Gyr respectively, not 2 Gyr. The two spikes are a discrete toy approximation, not a continuous inferred delay-time density.

units.boundary: Delay distributions depend strongly on which initial population and merger horizon were selected. A τ⁻¹-style illustrative distribution requires explicit lower and upper cutoffs before normalization, and observed cosmic rates additionally require cosmology and detection efficiency.

units.opening: Imagine running a population-synthesis model twice, once for low-metallicity progenitors and once for higher-metallicity progenitors. In each run you get a number of compact binaries that merge within a specified horizon. What you need for a fair comparison is not the raw count but the number of qualifying systems per amount of newly formed stellar mass that your simulation represents.

steps.heading: Define the numerator before calculating anything
steps.text: Choose the event class: for example, distinct black-hole binaries that merge within a stated time horizon. A binary that appears on ten event-log rows still contributes at most one qualifying system to a simple distinct-system numerator; a wide, bound double black hole may fail the merger-within-horizon criterion.

steps.heading: Find the physical denominator
steps.text: Let M_formed be the total formed stellar mass represented by the sampled birth population, including any prescribed correction for incomplete initial-mass or binary ranges. The formation efficiency η=N_merger/M_formed then has units of mergers per unit formed stellar mass. It is not dimensionless and is not automatically equal to a fraction of simulated systems.

steps.heading: Include weights and metallicity consistently
steps.text: If the sample uses proposal weights, compute a consistently weighted merger yield and the corresponding represented formed mass at each metallicity. Comparing η(Z₁) with η(Z₂) requires compatible birth distributions, outcome definitions, delay horizons and sample normalization; otherwise an apparent trend may reflect different simulation designs.

steps.heading: Do not skip the cosmic-rate and detector stages
steps.text: Formation efficiency answers how many merging systems arise per unit star formation under the model. To predict mergers per comoving volume per source-frame year, integrate it with cosmic star formation, birth-metallicity distributions and delay times. To predict detections, subsequently apply detector selection and observing exposure.

example.title: Counts alone are not efficiencies
example.text: A toy low-metallicity model yields 20 qualifying mergers representing 10,000 solar masses formed, giving η_low=20/10,000=0.002 mergers per solar mass. A higher-metallicity model yields 10 representing 20,000 solar masses, giving η_high=0.0005 mergers per solar mass. The yield ratio is four in this toy comparison, although the raw counts differ by only a factor of two.

units.boundary: The numerical comparison is constructed for teaching, not empirical evidence that low metallicity universally produces four times as many mergers. To interpret a physical efficiency, audit the initial-mass coverage, binary fraction, birth distributions, sample weights, metallicity modeling and the exact definition of a successful merger.

units.opening: Imagine an observed gravitational-wave signal that could have come from binaries with several plausible masses. You already have an astrophysical model specifying which masses are common, and you have a detector model telling you how well each candidate mass predicts the measured data. Bayesian inference combines the prior assumptions with the data likelihood.

steps.heading: Specify a parameter and what counts as data
steps.text: Let θ denote an unknown source parameter or a vector of masses, spins and distance, and d denote calibrated detector data. A likelihood p(d|θ) describes how probable the data would be under θ and the specified noise and waveform models. It is not a probability distribution over θ until you include a prior and normalize appropriately.

steps.heading: Use the prior explicitly rather than hiding it
steps.text: A prior p(θ) encodes assumptions about parameter values before conditioning on this particular data set. Bayes' theorem gives p(θ|d)=p(d|θ)p(θ)/p(d), where p(d)=∫p(d|θ)p(θ)dθ is the evidence for the specified model. A posterior summarizes updated uncertainty conditional on both likelihood and prior.

steps.heading: Interpret uncertainty and sensitivity
steps.text: A narrow posterior interval can result from informative data, a restrictive prior or both. Test sensitivity to defensible prior alternatives when drawing conclusions. Distinguish the posterior distribution for one event's parameters from a hierarchical population distribution whose hyperparameters describe a collection of events.

steps.heading: Connect posterior samples to population research
steps.text: A population model may reuse individual event samples, but the event-level priors used to generate those samples must be accounted for appropriately. A detected-event population likelihood also needs selection normalization; multiplying event posteriors without handling their priors and detection process can double-count assumptions or misrepresent the intrinsic population.

example.title: A discrete prior and likelihood update
example.text: Suppose a toy model has two possible states A and B with prior probabilities P(A)=0.2 and P(B)=0.8. An observation is three times as likely under A as under B: P(d|A)=0.6 and P(d|B)=0.2. Then P(A|d)=0.6×0.2/[0.6×0.2+0.2×0.8]=0.12/0.28≈0.429. The data moved A's probability from 20% to about 42.9%, but did not make A certain.

units.boundary: Bayesian probabilities are conditional on the stated hypothesis space, likelihood and prior. The discrete toy example is not a calibrated interpretation of detector strain or a proof of a physical formation channel; real analyses must handle waveform uncertainty, noise calibration and selection.

units.opening: Imagine opening a colleague's population-synthesis plot showing a steep decline in merger yield at high metallicity. You want to know whether you could obtain the same figure from the same inputs, and whether you could change one model assumption without accidentally changing five others. Reproducibility begins with knowing exactly what produced every data point.

steps.heading: Record the complete computational provenance
steps.text: For each run, record software and dependency versions, relevant model-prescription switches, random seeds, input-file identifiers, sample selection, units, analysis scripts and the environment needed to execute them. A screenshot of a plot or a link to an unspecified repository revision cannot establish which code and inputs created a result.

steps.heading: Track one system through the data model
steps.text: Before calculating rates, inspect the output schema and confirm what one row means. Event histories can have multiple entries per simulated binary, while outcome tables may have one row per system. Define distinct-system identifiers, join keys, sampling weights, formation metallicity and the field used to determine the merger outcome.

steps.heading: Reproduce a baseline before modifying assumptions
steps.text: Run the documented baseline with the available authorized inputs, recover a target quantity within stated numerical and stochastic tolerance, then change one independent variable at a time. Compare both raw diagnostics and normalized outcomes; any apparent physical trend could otherwise be a change in selection, data joins or units.

steps.heading: Describe discrepancies instead of making them vanish
steps.text: If your result differs from the documented reference, retain the discrepancy. Check units, missing values, seeds, version drift, event selection, binning, weighting and plotting code. Present a short evidence trail identifying which changes alter the result and which remain unexplained.

example.title: A single duplicate-ID bug can double a yield
example.text: Suppose an event log has IDs [11,11,11,19,23] and only system 11 meets the specified success condition. Counting successful rows gives 3, but counting successful distinct systems gives 1 out of 3 represented systems. A reproducible analysis should document the unit of observation and show how the data were deduplicated before normalizing by the represented formed stellar mass.

units.boundary: Reproducing a published or documented figure does not validate the underlying astrophysical model. Licensed datasets and authorized lab notebooks must be handled under their own access conditions. The Atlas cannot infer file schema, run COMPAS or certify reproducibility from a hypothetical example.

units.opening: Imagine looking backward through cosmic history and finding that the Universe formed stars at different rates at different epochs. A compact binary merging at one redshift may have come from stars born much earlier. To predict how many merging systems originate at each epoch, you need a formation history rather than a single present-day star-formation number.

steps.heading: Define what is being measured over cosmic time
steps.text: A cosmic star-formation-rate density ρ̇★(z) commonly denotes stellar mass formed per unit comoving volume per unit source-frame time at redshift z. Its units may be solar masses per year per cubic comoving megaparsec. That number differs from a galaxy's own star-formation rate because it describes the summed activity of a cosmic population per volume.

steps.heading: Separate birth rate from compact-binary formation efficiency
steps.text: A unit of newly formed stellar mass does not guarantee a compact binary will form and merge. Stellar initial masses, binary fraction, separation, metallicity and evolutionary prescriptions all influence how many successful merger-capable systems emerge. A formation efficiency per formed mass connects the cosmic birth history to the population model's yield.

steps.heading: Account for the time between birth and merger
steps.text: Each successful binary has a formation-to-merger delay, so mergers observed at one cosmic epoch receive contributions from several earlier birth epochs. A simple convolution of the formation history with a delay-time density illustrates this shift; a metallicity-dependent model integrates the birth-metallicity distribution at each formation epoch as well.

steps.heading: Convert the intrinsic merger history into observations
steps.text: An intrinsic comoving merger-rate density has units of mergers per comoving volume per source-frame time. Predicted detector counts need cosmological volume, the source-to-observer time factor, the observation duration and sensitivity to binary parameters; a direct comparison between a plotted cosmic star-formation curve and a detected-event histogram misses these transformations.

example.title: A deliberately discrete formation-to-merger example
example.text: A toy volume forms 1000 solar masses of stars at cosmic time 3 Gyr and 2000 solar masses at 6 Gyr. Suppose one merging compact binary forms per 1000 solar masses in each cohort and all such systems merge after a fixed 4-Gyr delay. The model produces one merger at 7 Gyr and two at 10 Gyr. This toy is a delayed accounting exercise, not a claim about actual cosmic star-formation rates or continuous merger-rate densities.

units.boundary: Published cosmic star-formation reconstructions depend on luminosity conversion, dust attenuation, stellar initial-mass functions and survey selection, among other choices. The rate density, cosmic-time/redshift conversion and detector selection must use mutually consistent cosmological and population conventions.

units.opening: Picture a donor star that has just begun losing material through its Roche-lobe boundary. There are two competing responses: the star itself changes radius as mass is removed, and the size of the gravitational region confining it also changes as mass ratio and orbit evolve. The difference between those responses can decide whether overflow settles down or accelerates.

steps.heading: Track donor-radius and Roche-radius changes separately
steps.text: Let R_d be the donor's radius and R_L its volume-equivalent Roche radius. Define logarithmic responses ζ_d=dlnR_d/dlnM_d and ζ_L=dlnR_L/dlnM_d for a specified mass-transfer timescale and orbital prescription. Because the donor is losing mass, dlnM_d is negative; the sign of a radius response must be interpreted with that negative change in mind.

steps.heading: Derive the local stability comparison
steps.text: Define overfill by the logarithmic ratio D=ln(R_d/R_L). For a small donor mass change, dD=(ζ_d−ζ_L)dlnM_d. If ζ_d>ζ_L and dlnM_d<0, the overfill decreases after the perturbation, a local stabilizing tendency under the chosen assumptions. If ζ_d<ζ_L, the donor increases its overfill and transfer may run away.

steps.heading: Specify which stellar response you are comparing
steps.text: A donor's immediate adiabatic response can differ markedly from its thermal-equilibrium radius adjustment. The Roche-radius response also depends on how much material the accretor retains and the angular momentum carried away by escaping gas. Stability therefore cannot be read from mass ratio alone without defining timescale, stellar structure and mass-transfer prescription.

steps.heading: Translate the local criterion into evolutionary possibilities
steps.text: An instability can lead to rapid mass loss, a common-envelope episode or a merger, but the local exponent comparison does not uniquely specify the final outcome. Stable transfer can strip a donor and modify its core and companion mass. Population-synthesis prescriptions approximate these pathways and should be tested against detailed stellar models where possible.

example.title: Read logarithmic radius exponents with the correct sign
example.text: Take a hypothetical mass decrement dlnM_d=−0.01, donor response ζ_d=+1 and Roche response ζ_L=−1. Then dD=(1−(−1))(−0.01)=−0.02: the logarithmic overfill decreases in this local toy model. Reversing the responses to ζ_d=−1 and ζ_L=+1 gives dD=+0.02, meaning overfill increases. These values are invented to explain signs, not tabulated exponents for any particular star.

units.boundary: The local ζ comparison is neither a complete dynamical calculation nor a universal critical-mass-ratio formula. The stellar envelope, thermal and dynamical timescales, spin, orbital evolution and matter-loss geometry determine which response is physically appropriate.

units.opening: Imagine receiving a simulated record of a binary containing only its component masses, separation and relative velocity at one instant. You want to predict the orbit it would follow if the two bodies were isolated point masses. Newton's gravitational force gives you a way to transform that snapshot into the shape and timing of an entire orbit.

steps.heading: Use the relative separation rather than following two trajectories independently
steps.text: Define r=r₂−r₁, M=m₁+m₂ and μ=m₁m₂/M. The relative separation obeys r̈=−GM r/r³ in the isolated Newtonian model, while the two stars move around their common center of mass. A plot centered on one of the stars is not a trajectory in a generally inertial frame.

steps.heading: Determine energy and angular momentum from a snapshot
steps.text: At separation r with relative velocity v, calculate the specific orbital energy ε=v²/2−GM/r and specific angular momentum h=|r×v|. Their values distinguish bound from unbound Kepler trajectories and, together with GM, determine the ellipse's semi-major axis and eccentricity when ε<0.

steps.heading: Connect orbital shape to the period
steps.text: For a bound ellipse, ε=−GM/(2a) and e²=1+2εh²/(GM)². The orbital period obeys T²=4π²a³/(GM), so doubling a at fixed masses lengthens the period by 2^(3/2), not by a factor of two. The orbital speed changes along an eccentric ellipse: the star moves faster near pericentre.

steps.heading: Check when this orbit model stops describing the binary
steps.text: Mass transfer, stellar winds, tides, supernova mass loss and gravitational radiation can modify the masses, orbital energy and angular momentum. Treat a Kepler ellipse as a useful instantaneous reference, then introduce those physical mechanisms to calculate how its orbital elements evolve.

example.title: Recover the period ratio for two binaries
example.text: Take two otherwise identical isolated circular binaries with separations a and 2a. Kepler's third law gives T₂/T₁=(2a/a)^(3/2)=√8≈2.828. Because the gravitational parameter GM is unchanged, an orbit twice as wide takes nearly three times as long. The numerical ratio does not depend on the individual masses as long as the same total mass is used in both cases.

units.boundary: Point-mass Kepler dynamics neglects the finite sizes of stars, hydrodynamic interaction, third bodies and gravitational-wave radiation. It does not supply a physical stellar-evolution history or guarantee that a compact pair with a particular semi-major axis will merge.

units.opening: Imagine following a massive star from the moment its core begins fusing hydrogen until its remaining core reaches a terminal state. The star does not stay in a single equilibrium configuration: energy generation, fuel depletion, changing composition, gravity and transport continually alter its internal structure and radius.

steps.heading: Identify which region is producing energy
steps.text: During core hydrogen burning, nuclear reactions convert hydrogen into helium and release energy that helps support the star against gravity. The balance is not simply that the surface is on fire: temperature, pressure, composition and energy transport through the interior determine the star's structure.

steps.heading: Follow core fuel depletion rather than only its surface color
steps.text: As the core's available hydrogen changes, the burning core's structure and the surrounding layers adjust. In later phases, shells can burn around a contracting core, and the outer envelope may expand. The evolution of a massive star depends on the coupled pressure, energy, composition and transport equations, not on a fixed sequence of surface labels.

steps.heading: Connect the star to its binary companion
steps.text: As the donor radius increases, it may reach the Roche-lobe boundary before completing its isolated-star evolution. Mass transfer can strip the envelope, alter the core-growth history and change the companion's mass. Tides, winds and orbital angular-momentum exchange may change whether that interaction begins at all.

steps.heading: Interpret the endpoint conditionally
steps.text: A massive star's final compact remnant depends on its evolved core, mass-loss history, composition, rotation, collapse and possible binary interaction. An initial mass by itself cannot uniquely specify a neutron-star or black-hole outcome; population synthesis uses explicit prescriptions or detailed-track interpolations to make that prediction.

example.title: A surface radius is enough to change the binary pathway
example.text: In an illustrative circular binary with an effective donor Roche-lobe radius of 40 solar radii, a star that expands from 20 to 50 solar radii crosses the geometric boundary during its evolution. A single-star track might have followed a different envelope history, but this binary can now transfer mass. Those radii alone do not determine whether transfer is stable or how much core mass survives.

units.boundary: Evolutionary stages and lifetimes depend on mass, composition, rotation, mixing and whether the star exchanges matter with a companion. This explanation is not a complete stellar structure calculation or a deterministic initial-mass-to-remnant-mass conversion.

units.opening: Imagine creating initial conditions for one million simulated binaries. If you draw primary masses uniformly between two limits, you will generally obtain a different population than if you sample the masses according to a power-law stellar birth distribution. The initial-mass function, or IMF, tells you how the assumed abundance of newly formed stars varies with mass.

steps.heading: Specify what a probability density means
steps.text: For a stellar mass m restricted to [m_min,m_max], let p(m) be a normalized density: ∫p(m)dm=1 across that interval. A common illustrative family is p(m)=C m^(−α). The constant C cannot be chosen until the lower and upper mass limits and the exponent are specified.

steps.heading: Normalize before sampling
steps.text: For α≠1, ∫m^(−α)dm=(m^(1−α))/(1−α), so C=(1−α)/(m_max^(1−α)−m_min^(1−α)). For α=1 the normalization is logarithmic. A density per unit mass is different from a density per logarithmic mass interval: dN/dlnm=m dN/dm.

steps.heading: Convert a fraction of stars into a mass normalization
steps.text: The number fraction in a mass interval is ∫p(m)dm over that interval. The expected formed mass per sampled star is E[m]=∫m p(m)dm; it is not the same as the number fraction. A simulation restricted to high-mass primaries may need a consistent correction for the lower-mass stars represented by the target star-forming population.

steps.heading: Connect birth masses to compact-object yield
steps.text: The IMF supplies one component of the initial binary distribution; you must separately specify binary fraction, mass ratio, period, eccentricity and correlations. Stellar and binary evolution convert these initial conditions to remnant outcomes. A high initial stellar mass increases neither survival nor detection probability by itself.

example.title: Normalize a very simple power law
example.text: Let p(m)=C m^(−2) for 1≤m≤10 in arbitrary mass units. Since ∫₁¹⁰m^(−2)dm=1−1/10=0.9, C=1/0.9=10/9. The number fraction in [5,10] is (10/9)∫₅¹⁰m^(−2)dm=(10/9)(1/5−1/10)=1/9≈11.1%. This toy IMF is not a claim about an observed stellar population.

units.boundary: An IMF is a model of births, not a distribution of present-day luminous stars or detected gravitational-wave sources. Its normalization and weighting conventions must match the binary-sampling scheme and any represented stellar-mass denominator.

units.opening: Imagine two massive stars born with the same initial mass but different chemical mixtures. In one of them, spectral-line absorption can transfer radiation momentum to atmospheric ions more efficiently, changing its wind history and pre-collapse mass. Metallicity is a useful part of this story, but it is not a unique label for every property of a star.

steps.heading: Define the composition precisely
steps.text: Astronomers often denote the hydrogen, helium and heavier-element mass fractions by X, Y and Z, with X+Y+Z=1. Here Z represents total mass fraction in elements heavier than helium. A reported oxygen abundance, iron abundance or logarithmic [Fe/H] is a different quantity and requires a composition model to translate into total Z.

steps.heading: Connect composition to a mechanism rather than a slogan
steps.text: In hot line-driven stellar winds, a variety of metal ions supply bound-bound transitions that can absorb/scatter stellar radiation and transfer momentum to gas. Under a specified range of stellar parameters, changing their abundance can alter mass-loss rates; which lines dominate depends on temperature and ionization. Metallicity also changes opacity and the stellar interior's evolutionary path.

steps.heading: Separate evolution of one star from the birth population
steps.text: A simulation's birth metallicity is an input condition; it may track surface and core abundances that change during evolution. The cosmic metallicity distribution is yet another object: a distribution of environments in which stars form at a given epoch. Using one representative metallicity at all redshifts can hide important population variation.

steps.heading: Trace how a metallicity assumption reaches merger predictions
steps.text: A different wind history can change the pre-collapse mass, envelope structure, orbital interaction and remnant mass. That may alter compact-binary survival and eventual gravitational-wave parameters. The path contains several model-dependent steps, so an observed high-mass merger cannot by itself uniquely establish the progenitor birth metallicity.

example.title: Mass fraction versus logarithmic abundance
example.text: Suppose a model changes total heavy-element mass fraction from Z=0.02 to Z=0.01 while keeping its defined reference composition otherwise fixed. It has halved this mass fraction, but that fact alone does not imply [Fe/H] fell by exactly log₁₀(2): the iron-to-hydrogen ratio and the assumed abundance pattern must also be specified. Do not interchange the two metallicity measures without a declared conversion.

units.boundary: Different abundance scales and wind prescriptions may use different solar reference mixtures, ionization regimes and metallicity variables. A simple metal-line wind scaling does not universally describe cool-star winds, eruptions, binary mass transfer or stellar-remnant formation.

units.opening: Imagine the iron-rich core of an evolved massive star no longer producing enough nuclear energy to support itself through further ordinary fusion. The core contracts under gravity, reaches extreme density and can form a proto-neutron star. The subsequent explosion and remnant properties depend on complicated neutrino transport, fluid dynamics and progenitor structure.

steps.heading: Understand the loss of support in the collapsing core
steps.text: A stellar core's pressure normally resists gravitational compression. In late burning stages, electron capture, photodisintegration and changes in the effective pressure response can contribute to collapse under suitable core conditions. This is not simply a star running out of every form of energy; the core's composition and equation of state matter.

steps.heading: Separate core bounce from a successful explosion
steps.text: Collapse is halted or strongly modified when the inner core reaches nuclear densities, producing a rebound and shock. The outgoing shock can lose energy to nuclear dissociation and neutrino emission. In many models, neutrino heating and multi-dimensional hydrodynamic instabilities help revive the shock; not every modeled core produces the same explosion.

steps.heading: Track what the binary experiences
steps.text: From a distant companion's perspective, the collapsed star's gravitational mass may decrease as matter and energy leave the system, and the new compact remnant can receive a recoil. Whether the binary stays bound depends on its pre-event relative orbit, the lost gravitational mass and the magnitude and direction of any natal kick.

steps.heading: Keep remnant predictions conditional
steps.text: A successful explosion, fallback, weak explosion or failed explosion may leave a neutron star or black hole depending on the progenitor core, equation of state and collapse prescription. The mapping from initial mass to remnant mass need not be monotonic across uncertain evolutionary and explosion regimes.

example.title: Apply only the post-event binary energy ledger
example.text: Consider a toy circular binary with initial GM=1 and r=1, so its relative speed is v=1. If a sudden symmetric collapse lowers the combined gravitational parameter to GM_final=0.6 and there is no kick, the post-event specific energy is ε=1/2−0.6=−0.1: it remains bound in the instantaneous point-mass toy model. This energy result does not predict the explosion's neutrino emission or ejecta dynamics.

units.boundary: Real core-collapse explosions are not instantaneous point-mass substitutions, and kicks can arise from asymmetric mass ejection or neutrino emission in model-dependent ways. Explosion mechanism, fallback and remnant identity require specialized simulations and observational constraints.

units.opening: Imagine returning to a binary after both original stars have ended their ordinary nuclear-burning evolution. The remaining objects could be white dwarfs, neutron stars or black holes. They are not interchangeable labels: their structure, compactness and maximum sustainable mass depend on distinct physical support mechanisms.

steps.heading: Start from what supports an ordinary star versus a remnant
steps.text: An ordinary star uses thermal and radiation pressure maintained through its evolutionary energy sources. A white dwarf is supported primarily by electron degeneracy pressure in its usual equilibrium regime. A neutron star involves dense nuclear matter and pressure from highly degenerate constituents, described by a relativistic equation of state.

steps.heading: Explain what makes a black hole qualitatively different
steps.text: A black hole possesses an event horizon beyond which outgoing signals cannot reach distant observers. The horizon is a causal boundary, not a solid surface in the stellar sense. A black hole's externally inferred mass and spin do not reveal a unique detailed record of the stellar envelope or collapse mechanism that produced it.

steps.heading: Connect progenitor evolution to the remnant distribution
