steps.text: Core mass, composition, winds, mass transfer and collapse physics alter which remnant type and mass a progenitor yields. Binary interactions can strip a massive star or accrete material onto an existing remnant. For population predictions, clearly separate the modeled progenitor distribution from the predicted remnant distribution.

steps.heading: Distinguish remnant formation from compact-merger formation
steps.text: Producing two compact objects in the same binary is not sufficient for a gravitational-wave merger within a finite cosmic age. The post-collapse system must remain bound and have an appropriate orbit. Its inspiral time depends strongly on separation and potentially eccentricity, while detection further depends on distance, masses and orientation.

example.title: The same remnant masses do not imply the same past
example.text: Two toy pathways may each produce a 10-solar-mass black hole: one via a single-star-like wind history and another after binary-envelope stripping followed by collapse. If a later gravitational-wave measurement constrains that black hole's mass near 10 solar masses, it has not directly distinguished these two histories. Additional distributions, spins, merger rates and population assumptions would be needed.

units.boundary: White-dwarf, neutron-star and black-hole outcome boundaries depend on the physical model and are not determined by one universal initial-mass threshold. Real remnant structure needs equations of state or strong-field gravity beyond this conceptual comparison.

units.opening: Imagine a pair of compact bodies orbiting around their common center of mass. Their overall center of mass may remain stationary, yet the arrangement of mass continually changes direction. In general relativity, the leading gravitational radiation for a slowly moving isolated source is connected to changes in its mass quadrupole rather than to an oscillating total mass.

steps.heading: Ask which mass moments can actually radiate
steps.text: For an isolated system, total mass-energy conservation constrains a time-varying mass monopole, while momentum conservation constrains the time evolution of the mass dipole associated with the center of mass. These conservation laws eliminate the corresponding leading radiation from those moments in the weak-field slow-motion treatment.

steps.heading: Construct an intuitive quadrupole tensor
steps.text: A quadrupole moment describes how mass is distributed with respect to two spatial directions. For point masses at positions x_A relative to a chosen origin, a trace-free form is Q_ij=Σ_A m_A(x_Ai x_Aj−δ_ij r_A²/3). As the binary rotates, this tensor changes even though its total mass and center-of-mass position remain constant.

steps.heading: Connect a time-changing moment to the distant wave
steps.text: In the leading weak-field transverse-traceless approximation, the far-zone radiative metric perturbation scales like h_ij^TT≈(2G/c⁴D) d²Q_ij^TT/dt² at retarded time, with conventions absorbed into the quadrupole definition. A circular binary's quadrupole orientation repeats after half an orbit, producing dominant wave frequency approximately twice the orbital frequency.

steps.heading: Follow the consequences of emitting radiation
steps.text: A changing quadrupole sends positive energy outward in gravitational waves. The orbit's energy becomes more negative as a quasi-circular compact binary inspirals, so the orbital frequency rises and its waveform chirps. More complete post-Newtonian and numerical-relativity calculations become necessary in stronger-field regimes.

example.title: Why the dominant wave cycles twice per orbit
example.text: For an idealized circular orbit, rotating both masses by 180 degrees returns the binary's mass-quadrupole pattern to the same orientation even though the bodies have each moved half an orbit. Therefore the leading quadrupolar waveform repeats twice per orbital period, and its leading gravitational-wave frequency is f_GW≈2f_orb. This is not a claim that every higher multipole or eccentric harmonic has that same frequency.

units.boundary: The quadrupole formula is a leading weak-field slow-motion approximation evaluated in an appropriate far-zone, transverse-traceless description. It cannot on its own reproduce the full merger-ringdown waveform or justify a gravitational-wave detection without an instrument and noise model.

units.opening: Imagine two astronauts carrying clocks along different routes between the same pair of spacetime events. The elapsed proper time they record may differ even though both begin and end at the same events. A metric describes how spacetime intervals are assigned to infinitesimal displacements and lets you integrate each clock's elapsed time along its worldline.

steps.heading: Treat coordinates as labels, not physical rulers
steps.text: An event has coordinate labels x^μ, but a coordinate difference does not by itself equal a measured spatial distance or elapsed clock time. The metric tensor g_μν(x) supplies the local relationship ds²=g_μν dx^μ dx^ν. Its components change when the coordinate system changes, while invariant intervals along physical paths retain their geometric meaning.

steps.heading: Follow a timelike worldline with a clock
steps.text: In the common signature (−,+,+,+), a timelike path satisfies ds²<0 and the clock's proper time obeys dτ=√(−ds²)/c. To find accumulated time, integrate dτ along the path; the result depends on the worldline, not only on differences between coordinate labels.

steps.heading: Use flat spacetime before introducing curvature
steps.text: In inertial Cartesian coordinates in flat spacetime, ds²=−c²dt²+dx²+dy²+dz². A clock moving at constant speed v relative to that frame accumulates dτ=dt√(1−v²/c²), illustrating why two differently moving clocks may record different proper times between events.

steps.heading: Connect geometry to gravitational waves without confusing positions with directions
steps.text: In curved spacetime, the metric varies with position and is determined dynamically by gravitational field equations under specified matter and boundary conditions. A gravitational wave is a propagating weak geometrical perturbation under appropriate conditions. Its predicted effect on separated freely falling bodies is connected to curvature and tidal relative acceleration, not to treating the position vector as the direction of the field.

example.title: Calculate a simple flat-spacetime clock reading
example.text: A spacecraft travels at v=0.6c for 10 years of inertial-coordinate time, with constant velocity during the interval. Its proper time is τ=10√(1−0.6²)=10×0.8=8 years. This is a simplified inertial-segment calculation; comparing clocks between the same departure and reunion events also requires accounting for the return route and any acceleration.

units.boundary: Metric-component values depend on coordinates, and a coordinate displacement is not generally a physical separation. The flat-spacetime example does not calculate curvature, strong-field clock behavior or a detector's real response to gravitational waves.

units.opening: Imagine asking a rapid population-synthesis code to create one hundred thousand newborn binaries. Before any star evolves, you must decide what combinations of primary mass, mass ratio, orbital period, eccentricity and metallicity enter the calculation. The distribution from which you sample these properties is already a physical assumption that can change the eventual merger predictions.

steps.heading: Write down the joint initial distribution
steps.text: Let θ_birth=(m₁,q,P,e,Z), where q=m₂/m₁ may be restricted by a declared primary-mass convention. A joint density p(θ_birth) describes the target birth population. Setting p(θ_birth)=p(m₁)p(q)p(P)p(e)p(Z) is an independence assumption, not a general statistical identity.

steps.heading: Check correlations and physical constraints
steps.text: Realistic or chosen binary distributions may correlate period and mass ratio, and eccentricity may depend on separation or stellar type. Some sampled combinations can violate Roche geometry or represent contact systems at birth. Define how the sampling method handles rejection, resampling or early interaction, since removing invalid draws changes the effective sample.

steps.heading: Track sample design versus intended population
steps.text: To increase computational efficiency, a code may oversample massive primaries or select only periods of interest. If the actual proposal distribution differs from the target population, attach weights or a documented normalization correction. Counting unweighted successful draws will then describe the simulation sampling strategy rather than the target birth distribution.

steps.heading: Propagate birth assumptions to observable predictions
steps.text: Evolving the draws through winds, transfer, collapse, kicks and inspiral produces remnant and merger distributions. Applying cosmic formation and detector selection then produces expected detections. A disagreement with observations cannot automatically be attributed to a late-stage physics prescription when the initial joint distribution is uncertain.

example.title: Independent sampling can forbid or invent a correlation
example.text: Suppose a toy birth model has two period categories, short and long, and two mass-ratio categories, equal and unequal, each marginally 50%. If you sample independently, each of the four combinations occurs with probability 25%. A different joint model may put 50% on short/equal and 50% on long/unequal, with zero probability for the other two combinations despite identical marginals. Such a difference can change which binaries interact.

units.boundary: An initial distribution cannot be inferred from its separate marginal histograms alone. Observational binary surveys have their own selection effects, and the code's proposal population, physical birth population and detector-selected merger population are distinct statistical objects.

units.opening: Imagine two cosmic epochs with the same total amount of star formation but different mixtures of metal-poor and metal-rich birth environments. If black-hole formation efficiency varies with the progenitor composition, the two epochs can produce different future merger histories even when their total new stellar mass is identical.

steps.heading: Represent metallicity as a distribution at each epoch
steps.text: Rather than assigning every newborn star one metallicity, define p(Z|t_birth) or a discrete weighted set of birth-metallicity bins. This distribution describes the fraction of star formation associated with each assumed composition at that epoch. A mean metallicity alone generally does not determine the effect of a nonlinear formation-efficiency function.

steps.heading: Weight each metallicity bin by its modeled yield
steps.text: Let η(Z) denote a compact-merger formation efficiency per unit formed stellar mass, under one specified population and delay convention. An epoch's effective yield is η_eff(t)=∫η(Z)p(Z|t)dZ. That integrates an astrophysical prescription over the birth-environment distribution; it is not an observed merger rate yet.

steps.heading: Add delay times and the cosmic formation history
steps.text: Progenitors born at one epoch can merge much later, so the modeled intrinsic merger-rate history combines the star-formation density, metallicity-dependent efficiency and delay-time distribution. The observable catalog further depends on detector selection and cosmological source-to-observer time conversion.

steps.heading: Identify what can and cannot be inferred
steps.text: Different metallicity histories, wind prescriptions and binary-interaction rules can produce overlapping merger-mass and rate predictions. Compare models across multiple observables and report degeneracies, rather than asserting a unique metallicity of birth for a single observed merger.

example.title: Why averaging metallicity before applying the yield can be wrong
example.text: Consider equal stellar-mass fractions at two toy metallicities Z₁ and Z₂ with efficiencies η(Z₁)=4 and η(Z₂)=1 in arbitrary mergers per mass units. The correct mixture yield is η_eff=0.5×4+0.5×1=2.5 units. Evaluating η only at the average metallicity (Z₁+Z₂)/2 need not equal 2.5 if η(Z) is nonlinear; the average of a function generally differs from the function of an average.

units.boundary: Metallicity distributions are model-dependent and may be uncertain in their low-metallicity tails. Yield values here are illustrative arbitrary units, and real predictions require consistent abundance definitions, normalization, star-formation history, delays and observational selection.

units.opening: Imagine compact objects moving in a dense star cluster, where close gravitational encounters are common. Two black holes that did not originate as the original components of one stellar binary may eventually become bound and merge after exchanges, binary hardening or other multi-body interactions. Their observed waveform can resemble a merger from an isolated binary, so formation history is an inference problem.

steps.heading: Distinguish pair formation from original stellar companionship
steps.text: In an isolated-binary channel, two stars evolve together through winds, transfer and collapse. In a dense dynamical environment, compact objects can interact after their progenitor stars have evolved, exchange partners in a pre-existing binary, form new bound systems and experience further encounters.

steps.heading: Follow the role of repeated gravitational interactions
steps.text: A binary passing near a third object can exchange energy and angular momentum. Under some encounter conditions a hard binary can become harder, transferring orbital energy to other bodies. Encounter rates depend on number density, velocity distribution, cluster structure and binary population rather than only on component masses.

steps.heading: Connect dynamics to the late inspiral
steps.text: An exchanged or hardened compact binary may later inspiral through gravitational-wave emission. Some dynamical encounters can produce eccentric sources or repeated mergers in suitable environments, but no one property uniquely proves dynamical formation. Stellar evolution, hierarchical mergers and detector selection introduce additional degeneracies.

steps.heading: Compare hypotheses through populations and environment
steps.text: Test predicted distributions of masses, spins, eccentricity, redshift and merger rates against observations under stated dynamical and isolated-channel models. An individual waveform constrains the merger's compact objects, not the full preceding chain of encounters; channels should be compared statistically and with careful selection modeling.

example.title: A toy energy transfer in a cluster encounter
example.text: Take an isolated Newtonian equal-mass compact binary with initial orbital energy E₁=−1 unit. After a hypothetical encounter, suppose its binary energy is E₂=−1.5 units. The binary has lost 0.5 unit of orbital energy; for total energy to balance, other components such as a recoiling intruder or the surrounding cluster must gain the corresponding energy, subject to any radiated losses. These arbitrary units illustrate an energy ledger, not an encounter simulation.

units.boundary: The frequency and outcomes of dynamical encounters require multi-body orbital integration and environmental modeling. A single merger mass or spin estimate does not determine its formation channel, and a simplified binary-energy comparison cannot predict a real cluster merger rate.
